tooley.q: A bus that supports the transfer of data in both directions is referred to as:
tooley.explain: A bus that can carry data both ways is called bidirectional (e.g. ARINC 629, AFDX, MIL-STD-1553); ARINC 429 by contrast is unidirectional only.
tooley.detail:
A bidirectional bus lets one line carry data in both directions (at different times), like ARINC 629, AFDX and MIL-STD-1553. "Universal" is not a term about direction and "asynchronous" describes synchronisation, not direction.

By contrast ARINC 429 is one-way: for two LRUs to exchange data both ways you need two separate 429 channels.

tooley.q: The main advantage of using a serial bus in an aircraft is:
opts: reduction in the size and weight of cabling
it supports the highest possible data rates
there is no need for data conversion
tooley.explain: A serial bus needs only one or two wire pairs instead of dozens of parallel wires, sharply cutting weight and installation space, matching reason #1 in the lecture slide (fewer wires, lower weight).
tooley.detail:
A serial bus sends bit by bit over one or two wire pairs, so it cuts the number of wires, weight and cable size, which is reason 1 of the lecture's six reasons for using buses. It does not remove the need for data conversion (serialisers and deserialisers are needed), and the highest possible speed is not its defining advantage.

Memory aid: serial means few wires, few wires means light.

tooley.q: Which one of the following is used to minimise reflections present in a bus cable:
tooley.explain: A terminating resistor (e.g. 78Ω at both ends of the ARINC 629 bus, per the lecture slide) absorbs the signal at the end of the cable, preventing reflections that would otherwise cause interference.
tooley.detail:
When a signal reaches the end of a line whose impedance does not match, part of it reflects back and distorts the data. A terminator equal to the cable's characteristic impedance absorbs the arriving signal so nothing reflects. The lecture gives 78 Ω at both ends of an ARINC 629 bus.

A coupler attaches devices to the bus; a shielded twisted pair rejects outside noise but does not deal with reflections.

tooley.q: The data format in an ARINC 429 stub cable consists of:
opts: parallel data from the local bus
tooley.explain: Per Tooley's own answer key, the ARINC 429 stub cable carries "serial analogue doublets": successive pairs of analogue voltage pulses, NOT Manchester-encoded data (easy to confuse, since Manchester is the encoding used by a different bus standard, ARINC 708/573).
tooley.detail:
Per Tooley's printed answer, the ARINC 429 stub cable carries "serial analogue doublets": pairs of analogue voltage pulses in series. People tend to answer Manchester, but Manchester belongs to ARINC 708, not 429. Parallel data from an internal bus is how data looks inside an LRU, not on the 429 cable.

Note: this question relies on the book's own wording; for study, just remember 429 is serial and uses BPRZ.

tooley.q: In order to represent negative data values, BNR data uses:
opts: BCD data and a binary sign bit
an extra parity bit to indicate the sign
tooley.explain: BNR (Binary Number Representation) encodes a signed integer using two's complement across the 19-bit Data field, with bit 29 (the Data field's MSB) acting as the sign bit.
tooley.detail:
BNR (Binary Number Representation) encodes signed integers in two's complement over the 19-bit Data field, with bit 29 (the MSB of Data) as the sign bit. BCD uses 4 bits per decimal digit with a separate sign, which is not how BNR shows negatives. A parity bit detects transmission errors; it does not indicate the sign of the data.

Example: -100 in 19-bit two's complement is 1111111111110011100.

tooley.q: The physical bus media specified in ARINC 629 is:
tooley.explain: ARINC 629 uses shielded twisted pair (STP) cable, physically similar to ARINC 429, but with a very different protocol (2 Mbps, bidirectional, no central bus controller needed).
tooley.detail:
ARINC 629 uses shielded twisted pair (STP), the same physical cable as ARINC 429 but a completely different protocol (2 Mbps, two-way, TDMA, no central controller). Fibre belongs to standards such as MIL-STD-1773B or FDDI; coaxial cable serves RF signals and ARINC 708.

Two standards can share one cable type; tell them apart by protocol, not by wire.

tooley.q: The validity of an ARINC 429 data word is checked by using:
tooley.explain: The last bit (bit 32) of the 32-bit word is an odd-parity bit: the total count of 1-bits across the whole word is always odd, letting the receiver detect simple single-bit errors.
tooley.detail:
The last bit (bit 32) of the 32-bit ARINC 429 word is odd parity: the number of 1s in the whole word is always odd, so the receiver only has to count to spot a single-bit error. Checksums and multiple redundancy belong to other systems (for example AFDX's CRC), not to a 429 word.

Limit: one parity bit cannot detect an even number of bit errors.

tooley.q: The label field in an ARINC 429 data word consists of:
tooley.explain: The Label occupies exactly 8 bits (bits 1-8), enough to encode 256 different data types (0-255), e.g. Label 203 = airspeed in the lecture's example label table.
tooley.detail:
The Label field is exactly 8 bits (bits 1 to 8), enough for 256 label values, for example Label 203 is indicated airspeed. 5 or 3 bits would be too few, and 8+2+19+2+1 = 32 shows the fields add up to the word length.

Tip: remember "Label 8, SDI 2, Data 19, SSM 2, Parity 1".

tooley.q: The voltages present on an ARINC 429 data bus cable are:
tooley.explain: Each conductor (A or B) carries +5V, 0V or -5V with respect to ground; only the DIFFERENTIAL voltage between the two wires reaches ±10V. The question asks about the voltage ON THE CABLE (each wire), so the answer is ±5V.
tooley.detail:
Each wire A or B carries +5 V, 0 V or -5 V relative to ground; only the differential voltage between the two reaches ±10 V. The question asks about the cable, i.e. each wire, so the answer is ±5 V. +5 V and +10 V lack the negative level; ±15 V is not a level of the standard.

Classic trap: mixing ±10 V (differential) with the voltage of each wire.

tooley.q: The maximum bit rate supported by ARINC 429 is:
tooley.explain: ARINC 429 has two speeds: low speed 12.5 kbps (most common) and high speed 100 kbps, which is the MAXIMUM rate supported.
tooley.detail:
ARINC 429 has two speeds: low 12.5 kbps (the most common) and high 100 kbps. The maximum supported is 100 kbps. 12.5 kbps is the low speed, and 1 Mbps is the MIL-STD-1553 figure.

Transmitting one word at 100 kbps takes 32/100,000 = 0.32 ms.

tooley.q: An ARINC 429 NULL state is represented by:
tooley.explain: NULL (no data present) corresponds to both wires A and B sitting at 0V, distinct from bit 1 (A=+5V, B=-5V) and bit 0 (A=-5V, B=+5V).
tooley.detail:
NULL is the no-data state: both wires A and B at 0 V. Bit 1 is A = +5 V, B = -5 V; bit 0 is A = -5 V, B = +5 V (reversed). Because a NULL state always sits between bits, the code is called Return to Zero.

Remember: NULL is not the same as a 0 bit.

tooley.q: The maximum data rate supported by MIL-STD-1553 is:
tooley.explain: MIL-STD-1553B supports 1 Mbps, faster than ARINC 429 (max 100 kbps) but slower than ARINC 629 (2 Mbps) and AFDX (100 Mbps).
tooley.detail:
MIL-STD-1553B supports 1 Mbps: faster than ARINC 429 (up to 100 kbps) but slower than ARINC 629 (2 Mbps) and AFDX (100 Mbps). The other two options (12.5 kbps, 100 kbps) are ARINC 429 speeds.

Speed order: 429 < 1553 < 629 < AFDX.

tooley.q: A bus that is self-clocking is referred to as:
tooley.explain: ARINC 429's BPRZ encoding always has a transition in the middle of every bit (return to 0V), so the receiver can recover timing from the signal itself with no separate clock wire: this is the self-clocking property.
tooley.detail:
BPRZ coding always has a transition to 0 V between bits, so the receiver recovers timing from the data signal itself with no separate clock wire: this is the self-clocking property. Tooley uses the word "asynchronous" for this idea (no shared clock line between the two ends). "Bidirectional" and "universal" have nothing to do with timing.

Note the answer follows the book's wording.

tooley.q: The physical bus media specified in MIL-STD-1773B is:
tooley.explain: MIL-STD-1773B is the fibre-optic implementation of MIL-STD-1553B, giving much greater immunity to high-intensity radiated electromagnetic fields (HIRF) than copper cable.
tooley.detail:
MIL-STD-1773B is the fibre-optic version of MIL-STD-1553B, giving much better immunity to electromagnetic interference and HIRF than copper. Coaxial and shielded twisted pair are the physical media of copper standards (1553B uses shielded twisted pair).

Tip: 1773 is 1553 on optical fibre.

tooley.q: The length of an ARINC 429 word is:
tooley.explain: An ARINC 429 word is always 32 bits long: Label(8)+SDI(2)+Data(19)+SSM(2)+Parity(1) = 32.
tooley.detail:
An ARINC 429 data word is always 32 bits: Label 8 + SDI 2 + Data 19 + SSM 2 + Parity 1 = 32. 16 and 20 bits are not the standard's size. ARINC 629 has the 52-bit frame.

Keep 32 for the transmission time t = 32/R.

tooley.q: ARINC 573 is designed for use with:
tooley.explain: ARINC 573 is the standard for Flight Data Recorders (FDR), using 12-bit Harvard Bi-Phase encoding; ARINC 717 later superseded ARINC 573.
tooley.detail:
ARINC 573 is the standard for flight data recorders (FDR), using Harvard Bi-Phase coding at 12 bits; ARINC 717 later replaced it. Inertial navigation and weather radar use other standards (weather radar is ARINC 708).

Three to tell apart: 573/717 = FDR, 708 = weather radar, 429 = basic avionics.

tooley.q: The maximum data rate supported by the FDDI bus is:
tooley.explain: FDDI (Fibre Distributed Data Interface), developed by Boeing for the 777, supports 100 Mbps over a dual token-ring topology.
tooley.detail:
FDDI (Fibre Distributed Data Interface), developed by Boeing for the B777, supports 100 Mbps on a dual token-ring structure. 1 Mbps is the 1553 figure and 10 Mbps is ordinary Ethernet, not FDDI. ARINC 636 for the 777's optical network was adapted from FDDI (Module 08).

Remember: FDDI = 100 Mbps, dual ring, optical fibre.

floyd.q: A bus connects two or more devices to allow them to communicate.
floyd.detail: Floyd section 13-6: a bus is a shared path over which devices exchange data; it is also described by characteristics such as width, frequency, transfer rate and bandwidth. It is the same idea as Module 05's "data bus", except Floyd treats general computer buses rather than avionics.

floyd.q: A bus is only defined by the wires and connectors.
floyd.explain: False: a bus is also defined by protocol, data rate and encoding.
floyd.detail: Floyd Self-Test question 23 answer (d): the properties defining a bus include connector type, cable length and type, data rate and encoding. Compare ARINC 429: its wire (shielded twisted pair) is the same as ARINC 629 but the protocol differs, so you cannot judge from the wire alone.

floyd.q: A parallel bus is always faster than a serial bus.
floyd.explain: False: a parallel bus is limited by crosstalk, EMI and clock skew.
floyd.detail: Floyd 13-6: parallel bus speed can be limited by crosstalk, EMI and clock skew, so modern serial buses can reach higher speeds on fewer wires. This is exactly why avionics uses serial buses (few wires, light, low noise) in Module 05.

floyd.q: Bus width is the width of each conductor in a parallel bus.
floyd.explain: False: bus width is the number of lines (bits) of the bus.
floyd.detail: Bus width is the number of parallel data lines, for example an 8-bit bus has 8 lines. It is one of the four characteristics Floyd names: width, frequency, transfer rate and bandwidth. Transfer rate = width × frequency (when one word moves per cycle).

floyd.q: Handshaking is not a part of the bus protocol.
floyd.explain: False: handshaking is part of the protocol.
floyd.detail: Floyd defines a handshake as the routine by which two devices initiate and complete a bus transfer; the bus protocol is the set of rules for establishing and maintaining communication, which includes handshaking.

floyd.q: A single-ended transmission is simpler and lower in cost compared to a differential transmission.
floyd.explain: True: single-ended uses one signal wire plus ground; differential uses two complementary wires.
floyd.detail: Single-ended needs only one data wire and a ground so it is cheap and simple but noise-sensitive. Differential sends the signal and its complement on two wires and the receiver takes the difference, which rejects common-mode noise well; that is why ARINC 429 uses ±5 V on wires A and B.

floyd.q: A tri-state driver has a HIGH state, a LOW state, and a shorted state.
floyd.explain: False: the third state is high impedance (open), not shorted.
floyd.detail: In the high-impedance state the device is disconnected from the bus, so many devices can share one line without conflict (Floyd 13-10). A short would damage the whole bus. It links to "bus contention" and arbitration in Tooley.

floyd.q: PCI stands for peripheral computer interface.
floyd.explain: False: PCI is peripheral component interconnect.
floyd.detail: Self-Test question 26 (answer (d)). The two PCI types are PCI-X and PCI-E (PCI Express, PCIe); in PCIe the individual paths from the switch to peripherals are called lanes (Self-Test question 27, answer (b)).

floyd.q: Two types of PCI buses are PCI-X and PCI-E.
floyd.detail: PCI-X is the extended parallel bus and PCI-E (PCI Express) is the serial bus using lanes. Floyd Section Checkup 13-7 notes PCI-Express is also written PCIe and PCI-E, and a lane is a dedicated path to a single chip called a switch.

floyd.q: IEEE-488 is known as the GPIB.
floyd.explain: True: GPIB is the general-purpose interface bus per IEEE-488.
floyd.detail: GPIB is a parallel bus used to connect laboratory instruments. Floyd 13-7 also mentions SCSI (small computer system interface) in the same parallel bus group.

floyd.q: SCSI stands for serial computer system interface.
floyd.explain: False: SCSI is small computer system interface.
floyd.detail: Floyd 13-7: SCSI is small computer system interface; the serial version is called serial SCSI (among the other serial buses of 13-9). The first S is "small", not "serial".

floyd.q: USB is a widely used standard serial bus for connecting peripherals to a computer.
floyd.detail: USB (universal serial bus) has pins D+, D-, +5 V and ground; the twisted pair D+ and D- carries half-duplex differential data in versions up to 2.0, while USB 3.0 adds two more twisted pairs and is full-duplex (Floyd 13-8).

floyd.q: The SPI bus is typically used in embedded systems and on PCBs between microprocessors or microcontrollers and peripheral ICs.
floyd.explain: True: SPI is the serial peripheral interface.
floyd.detail: In the same group of short on-board serial buses is I2C (inter-integrated circuit). Floyd's statement 40 asks which internal serial bus mainly connects ICs on a PCB; the answer is I2C.

floyd.q: Most automotive systems use the Firewire bus.
floyd.explain: False: automotive systems use the CAN bus.
floyd.detail: CAN is the controller area network, a serial bus made of a terminated twisted pair; cars usually have two CAN buses, one low-speed and one high-speed. Firewire is IEEE-1394, a high-speed external bus developed by Apple (Floyd 13-9). Tooley covers the aircraft counterparts: ARINC 429, 629.

floyd.q: CAN stands for computer area node.
floyd.explain: False: CAN is controller area network.
floyd.detail: Self-Test question 32 (answer (b)): the bus typically used to connect systems in an automobile is the CAN. Tip: the first C is controller.

floyd.explain: USB 3.0 has the 2.0 twisted pair D+/D- plus two more twisted pairs.
floyd.detail:
Versions up to 2.0 have one twisted pair carrying half-duplex data. USB 3.0 adds two twisted pairs (one for receiving, one for high-speed sending) so it is full-duplex with SuperSpeed 4.8 Gbps; 9 contacts instead of 4. Three twisted pairs in all.

The twisted pairs reduce or remove noise, as in Section Checkup 13-8.

floyd.q: Which of the following is NOT a USB speed classification?
floyd.explain: USB has four speed classes: low, full, high, super; there is no "intermediate".
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.13 · Self-Test #28 (printed key (b), site uses (d))
floyd.detail:
Floyd section 13-8 lists four USB speed classes: low-speed, full-speed, high-speed and super-speed. So "intermediate speed" is the option not on the list.

PRINTING ERROR NOTE: Floyd's answer key gives (b) for this question, but full-speed is a real class so (b) cannot be the answer; per the chapter's own text the correct answer is (d) intermediate speed. The site uses this correct answer.

floyd.q: The bus typically used to connect systems in an automobile is the:
floyd.detail:
SPI and I2C connect ICs on a board and PCI connects computer peripherals. CAN is a two-wire twisted-pair serial bus with terminating resistors, tolerant of noise, designed for noisy environments such as cars.

In aviation the corresponding role is played by ARINC 429, 629 and AFDX.

floyd.q: Properties that define a bus include:
opts: all of these: connector type, cable length and type, data rate and encoding
floyd.explain: Floyd Self-Test question 23: answer (d) all of these.
floyd.detail:
A bus is defined by several things at once: connectors, cable (length and type), data rate and encoding, plus protocol. Picking a single property is incomplete.

Application: two buses with the same twisted-pair cable still differ if their speed and encoding differ (429 versus 629).

generated.q: ARINC 629 supports a data transmission rate of:
generated.explain: ARINC 629 reaches 2 Mbps, 20 times faster than ARINC 429's top speed (100 kbps), matching the figures in the lecture slide.
generated.detail:
ARINC 629 reaches 2 Mbps, 20 times the top speed of ARINC 429 (100 kbps). 100 kbps belongs to 429 and 100 Mbps to AFDX, so those options mix up standards.

Comparison axis: 429 (100 kbps) → 629 (2 Mbps) → AFDX (100 Mbps).

generated.q: The channel access mechanism used by ARINC 629 is:
generated.explain: ARINC 629 uses TDMA: each LRU is assigned one or more fixed time slots within a Major Frame to transmit, avoiding data collisions without needing a central bus controller.
generated.detail:
TDMA divides time into fixed slots; each LRU transmits in its own slot of the Major Frame, so there are no collisions without a central controller. CSMA/CD is half-duplex Ethernet's mechanism (listen then transmit, with collisions), and Token Ring passes a token; neither is ARINC 629.

Recompute the cycle: 125 slots × 16 µs = 2 ms.

generated.q: AFDX (ARINC 664) achieves a maximum transmission rate of:
generated.explain: AFDX is 100 Mbps switched full-duplex Ethernet, using the Virtual Link (VL) mechanism to guarantee deterministic bandwidth for each data flow.
generated.detail:
AFDX is switched full-duplex Ethernet at 100 Mbps. 2 Mbps is ARINC 629 and 1 Mbps is MIL-STD-1553. The lecture's comparison table ranks AFDX fastest of the four.

Implication: large data such as maintenance images or video only fits on AFDX.

generated.q: In AFDX, the mechanism that guarantees each data flow its own bandwidth, preventing other flows from consuming it, is called:
generated.explain: Each Virtual Link has its own bandwidth, frame size and transmission period (BAG); the AFDX switch isolates VLs from each other so that one faulty flow cannot congest the whole network.
generated.detail:
A Virtual Link (VL) is a logical channel in the physical AFDX network; each VL has its own bandwidth, frame size and BAG period, and the switch isolates VLs so one flow cannot take another's bandwidth. A Label is ARINC 429's data identifier and the TDMA slot belongs to 629.

VLs are why AFDX can be deterministic although it is Ethernet.

generated.q: A central bus controller is a required component of which of the following bus standards?
generated.explain: MIL-STD-1553B uses a command-response architecture with one Bus Controller (BC) managing up to 31 Remote Terminals (RT); ARINC 629, by contrast, was designed to need NO central bus controller (avoiding a single point of failure).
generated.detail:
MIL-STD-1553B uses a command-response architecture: one Bus Controller (BC) controls up to 31 Remote Terminals (RT). ARINC 629 is the opposite, designed to need no central controller (avoiding a single point of failure), and ARINC 429 has no controller because it is point-to-point and one-way.

The BC is also a weak point: if it fails the whole bus stops, so 1553 usually has a backup BC.

generated.q: The SSM field in an ARINC 429 data word is used to:
opts: identify the type of data being transmitted
specify which device receives the data
report data status (valid, failure, test mode...)
generated.explain: SSM (Sign/Status Matrix, 2 bits) reports one of 4 context-dependent data states, e.g. for BNR: 00=Failure Warning, 01=No Computed Data, 10=Functional Test, 11=Normal Operation.
generated.detail:
The SSM (Sign/Status Matrix, 2 bits) reports the status of the data itself: for BNR, 00 is Failure Warning, 01 is No Computed Data, 10 is Functional Test, 11 is Normal Operation. The data type is given by the Label and the intended receiver by the SDI.

Engineers never judge data from the Data field alone; they look at the SSM first.

generated.q: If a 32-bit ARINC 429 word is transmitted at 100 kbps, the time to transmit one word is:
generated.explain: t = N/R = 32 bits / 100,000 bit/s = 0.00032 s = 0.32 ms, matching the Data Rate and Bit Timing table in the lecture slide.
generated.detail:
t = N/R = 32 bits / 100,000 bit/s = 0.00032 s = 0.32 ms. 3.2 ms is off by a factor of 10, and 2.56 ms is the result at the low speed of 12.5 kbps (32/12,500).

Quick check: the high speed is 8 times the low speed, so the time is 8 times shorter (2.56/8 = 0.32).

generated.q: With 6 sensors each sending its own data to 4 displays, how many wires does point-to-point need, and how many does a shared bus need (1 wire per device)?
generated.explain: Point-to-point: 6 × 4 = 24; shared bus: 6 + 4 = 10.
generated.detail:
Point-to-point grows as the product n × m because each sensor needs its own wire to each display. A shared bus grows as the sum n + m because each device connects one wire to the bus. With 6 and 4 that is 24 versus 10.

Add one new sensor: point-to-point needs 4 more wires, the bus only 1. The gap widens as devices increase, which is reason 1 of the six reasons for buses.

generated.q: How many receivers can one ARINC 429 transmitter feed at most?
generated.explain: ARINC 429 is a one-way bus: 1 transmitter feeds at most 20 receivers.
generated.detail:
This is ARINC 429's multi-drop property: one transmitter, several receivers (for example the ADIRU transmits and the FMGC, FWC and DMC all receive). But data only flows one way, so a return path needs a second channel.

The limit of 20 comes from the electrical loading of the line: each receiver is a load.

generated.q: Why does an LRU such as the ADIRU have both Tx and Rx pins although ARINC 429 is a one-way bus?
opts: Because each 429 channel carries one direction, so sending and receiving are separate channels
Because the ADIRU reverses the bus direction when needed
Because each wire of one 429 channel runs in a different direction
generated.explain: Two-way exchange needs two separate one-way channels.
generated.detail:
One 429 channel is a wire pair A, B that together carry a differential signal from transmitter to receivers; the two wires do not run in opposite directions. The ADIRU sends air data to the FMGC on one channel and receives commands from the FMGC on another, so it has both Tx and Rx.

A complex LRU may have dozens of Tx/Rx channels, each a one-way flow.

generated.q: The differential voltage between wires A and B of ARINC 429 when sending a 1 is:
generated.explain: Bit 1: A = +5 V, B = -5 V so A - B = +10 V.
generated.detail:
The receiver only measures the difference A - B. A 1 gives +10 V, a 0 gives -10 V, NULL gives 0 V. With a differential signal, noise acting almost equally on both wires cancels when the difference is taken.

+5 V is the voltage of one wire relative to ground, not the differential voltage; 0 V is the NULL state.

generated.q: Why does BPRZ coding let the receiver do without a separate clock line?
opts: Because BPRZ sends the clock on a hidden second wire pair
Because BPRZ runs faster than the receiver's clock
Because every bit has a rising and a falling edge, so there is always a reference to count timing
generated.explain: The transition in every bit lets timing be recovered (self-clocking).
generated.detail:
With a non-return-to-zero code (NRZ), the string 1111 holds +10 V across four bits so there is no edge to show the bit boundaries and timing drifts easily. BPRZ always returns to 0 V between bits, so even 1111 has a rising and falling edge in every bit.

The price: higher switching frequency than NRZ at the same bit rate.

generated.q: Which bit is the Parity field of an ARINC 429 word, and what kind of parity is it?
generated.explain: Parity is bit 32 (sent last), odd parity.
generated.detail:
Bit 1 is the first bit of the Label and is sent first; bit 32 is the Parity and is sent last. Bit 29 is the sign/MSB of the BNR Data field. Rule: the total number of 1s in all 32 bits must be odd; an even count means an error.

The sender sets Parity = 0 if the first 31 bits already have an odd number of 1s, otherwise 1.

generated.q: What is the 2-bit SDI field of an ARINC 429 word used for?
opts: Distinguishing the source or destination further within the same Label
Reporting whether the data is valid or failed
generated.explain: The SDI (Source/Destination Identifier) extends how many channels one Label can tell apart.
generated.detail:
The Label has only 8 bits (256 values) so it cannot separate every source and destination for the same kind of data. The SDI adds 2 bits to say, for example, whether this IAS belongs to ADIRU 1, 2 or 3. Data status is reported by the SSM and transmission errors are caught by the Parity.

Three fields, three jobs: the Label says what, the SDI says whose, the SSM says whether it can still be trusted.

generated.q: The BCD encoding of an airspeed of 250 kt, digit by digit 2, 5, 0, is:
generated.detail:
BCD encodes each decimal digit separately with 4 binary bits, so 250 becomes three 4-bit groups. 0110 is the digit 6 and 0001 is the digit 1, so the other options encode wrong digits.

Three BCD digits need 12 bits, which fits the 19-bit Data field; five digits need 20 bits and do not fit (a point to be careful about).

generated.q: In BNR Data format, which bit is the sign bit?
opts: Bit 29, the highest bit of the Data field
Bit 11, the lowest bit of the Data field
generated.explain: The Data field occupies bits 11 to 29; bit 29 is the MSB and the sign bit of the two's-complement number.
generated.detail:
Field order: Label bits 1 to 8, SDI bits 9 to 10, Data bits 11 to 29, SSM bits 30 to 31, Parity bit 32. A two's-complement number has its sign bit at its highest position, bit 29: 0 is positive, 1 is negative. Bit 32 is the Parity.

These bit ranges add up to 8 + 2 + 19 + 2 + 1 = 32, matching the word length.

generated.q: How many bits does an ARINC 629 frame have and which fields?
opts: 32 bits: Label 8, SDI 2, Data 19, SSM 2, Parity 1
52 bits: Sync 8, Data 32, SDI 2, Label 8, SSM 2
generated.explain: 8 + 32 + 2 + 8 + 2 = 52 bits; 32 bits with Parity is ARINC 429.
generated.detail:
The 629 frame adds an 8-bit Sync field to synchronise frames in a TDMA system with many LRUs sharing a bus, and has 32 Data bits instead of 19. The Label, SDI and SSM fields match 429 in size and meaning, showing 629 inherits from 429.

The second option describes a 429 word and the third is an invented number.

generated.q: In ARINC 629, how long is a Major Frame and how many slots does it have (per the lecture)?
opts: 16 ms with 125 slots of 128 µs each
2 ms with 16 slots of 125 µs each
2 ms with 125 slots of 16 µs each
generated.detail:
The arithmetic checks: 125 × 16 = 2000 µs = 2 ms. The other options swap or mis-multiply (125 × 128 µs = 16 ms is correct arithmetic but not the lecture's figure; 16 × 125 µs is also 2 ms but swaps the slot count and slot length).

Remember the lecture's figures: 125 slots, 16 µs, 2 ms, up to 20 to 21 LRUs.

generated.q: In AFDX, what is the BAG (Bandwidth Allocation Gap)?
opts: The number of switches between two devices
The minimum time between two consecutive frames of a Virtual Link
The maximum size of an Ethernet frame
generated.explain: The BAG sets a VL's minimum period, which is how bandwidth is guaranteed.
generated.detail:
Each VL has its own BAG; it limits how often the VL may send and, with the maximum frame size, sets the bandwidth granted to the VL. The switch polices it so no VL exceeds its share. This is separate from frame size (another parameter) and the number of switches (network architecture).

Example: a 1500-byte maximum frame with a 4 ms BAG gives a maximum bandwidth of 1500 × 8 / 0.004 = 3 Mbps.

generated.q: A FADEC must send small amounts of engine data with very high reliability in a noisy environment. Which of the four standards fits best?
opts: MIL-STD-1553 (or ARINC 717), the dedicated bus for engines
generated.explain: The lecture assigns FADEC ↔ engine to MIL-STD-1553/ARINC 717.
generated.detail:
Engine data is small (little bandwidth) but needs high reliability with a deterministic central controller, so a dedicated command-response bus such as 1553 fits; AFDX is for large-volume data and 629 for real-time flight control. Fastest does not mean best fit.

The self-check at the end of Module 05 asks exactly this situation.

generated.q: How does electromagnetic noise act on a twisted pair and why does a differential signal tolerate it?
opts: The twisted pair absorbs the noise completely
Noise acts almost equally on both wires, so the difference A - B barely changes
Noise acts only on wire A
generated.explain: Common-mode noise cancels when the two wires are subtracted.
generated.src: Data Buses lecture · relevant part; Tooley 14.6.3
generated.detail:
Because the two wires are twisted tightly they sit in the same noise field and pick up the same noise voltage (common-mode noise). The receiver takes the difference A - B so the common part cancels and only the signal remains. Nothing absorbs it "completely" and noise does not hit one wire only.

This is also the principle behind common-mode filters in Module 09.

generated.q: In the lecture's A320 diagram, over which bus does the ADIRU send data to the FMGC?
generated.explain: Air and inertial data from the ADIRU travels over ARINC 429.
generated.detail:
The lecture assigns: ADIRU → FMGC over ARINC 429; ELAC, SEC, FAC over ARINC 629; FMGC, ECAM, CIDS, ACMS over AFDX; FADEC and engines over 1553/717. Basic sensor data with little bandwidth suits 429 well.

Also remember: ARINC 429 is both the slowest and the most widely used because it is simple, cheap and very reliable.

generated.q: Slide 14 of the Data Buses lecture says ARINC 429 uses Manchester Biphase-L coding. Is that right or wrong, and why?
opts: Right but only at the high speed
Wrong: ARINC 429 uses BPRZ, Manchester belongs to ARINC 708
generated.explain: Two other slides of the same lecture and Tooley both confirm BPRZ.
generated.src: Data Buses lecture · slides 3, 13, 14; Tooley ch.4
generated.detail:
Slides 3 and 13 of the lecture and Tooley (Electrical characteristics and the BPRZ glossary entry) all say ARINC 429 coding is Bipolar Return to Zero. Manchester is ARINC 708's (weather radar) code. "Only at the high speed" is invented.

This is an example of always cross-checking sources before memorising a technical fact.

generated.q: Two ARINC 429 devices want to exchange data both ways. How many 429 channels are needed at least?
opts: 4 channels because each wire is a channel
generated.explain: Each channel is one-way so two-way needs two channels.
generated.detail:
A 429 channel is one wire pair for one direction. For A to send to B and B to send to A you need an A→B channel and a B→A channel. A wire pair cannot become two channels, so 4 is wrong; "1 two-way channel" contradicts the definition.

Compare 629: two-way on the same bus thanks to TDMA.

generated.q: Which ordering lists the four buses by increasing speed?
generated.explain: 100 kbps < 1 Mbps < 2 Mbps < 100 Mbps.
generated.detail:
In the same unit: ARINC 429 at most 0.1 Mbps, MIL-STD-1553 1 Mbps, ARINC 629 2 Mbps, AFDX 100 Mbps. The other orderings swap a pair.

Do not confuse speed order with importance: 429 is slowest but most widely used.

generated.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the reasons for using data buses on aircraft?
opts: Increasing the number of wires for more redundancy
Fewer wires, less weight and space
generated.explain: A bus reduces wire count; redundancy comes from independent buses, not from more wires.
generated.detail:
Six reasons: fewer wires, data sharing, higher reliability (independent A/B buses), easier maintenance and fault isolation, easier expansion, support for several data types. More wires is exactly what buses exist to avoid.

Note the word NOT: this is an elimination-type question.
